archetype.name: Better Than Its Record (defense-first)
archetype.definition: A team whose top-ten defense and luckless close-game results make it better than 0-6, but whose last-ranked offense still makes it a bottom-tier side rather than a sleeping contender.

report.headline: A top-ten defense chained to the league's worst offense, and nothing breaking right
report.take:
The Chargers were supposed to be good. The Book made them 8.5- and 6.5-point home favorites in the first two weeks, and they lost both 14-26. Six weeks in they are 0-6, last in an AFC West led by an unbeaten Kansas City. The two winning seasons before this one were built on defense, and the defense is still mostly there. Nearly everything else has collapsed.

The offense is the story. It ranks 32nd in EPA per play, 32nd in passing EPA and 30th in success rate, and it scores 15 points a game. The root is protection. A 9.5% sack rate ranks 31st, Justin Herbert has gone down 21 times, and the line commits 5.3 penalties a game, the most in the league. Harbaugh has responded by hiding the pass. A pass rate 11.4 points under expectation is the most run-heavy approach in football. But the run game is worse per play than the passing game: run EPA of -0.235 ranks 28th and run success ranks 24th. So the plan leans on the weaker unit and puts Herbert into obvious passing downs behind a leaky line. The passing game has sunk week by week and bottomed out in a 6-22 loss at Kansas City.

The record overstates how bad the team is, though not by much. Wins over expected of -2.62 is the worst in the league: the point differential implies 2.6 wins against zero actual, and they are winless in one-score games. The defense is better than its 25.2 points allowed suggests. It ranks 9th in EPA allowed, 5th on third down and 6th in the red zone. Fifteen giveaways have kept handing opponents short fields. Still, a -10.2 per-game differential belongs to a bad team, not a coin-flip team that got unlucky. Turning the record around takes a working offense, not just better bounces.

The near term depends on the infirmary. Joe Alt and Kayode Awosika are out on the line, Tre' Harris is out at receiver, Ladd McConkey is in the concussion process, and Derwin James is out in the secondary. All carry return estimates that land on the Rams game, and those are estimates, not promises. The middle of the schedule softens with Houston, the Jets, Tampa and a winless Miami. The finish of San Francisco, Kansas City and Denver does not. The playoffs are realistically gone. What remains open is whether the offense can find a floor.

strengths.title: Defense that wins the money downs
strengths.body: This unit gets off the field. It ranks 5th on third down, 6th in red-zone touchdown rate and 9th in EPA allowed, despite constantly defending short fields. That matches the 2024 and 2025 defenses, which ranked 5th and 6th in EPA allowed, so it is a durable identity rather than a six-game blip.

strengths.title: Takeaways keep games within reach
strengths.body: Ten takeaways rank 3rd in the league and are the main reason losses have stayed mostly one- or two-score games. The total is lumpy: five came in a single afternoon at Buffalo. Expect the rate to cool toward average, so this is a genuine asset that will contribute less going forward.

strengths.title: Hits the QB, smothers the short game
strengths.body: The rush converts pressure into contact, with a QB hit rate ranking 8th, even though the sack total is only mid-pack. Paired with short-pass defense ranked 9th by EPA, this makes it hard to dink and dunk against them. That is how the third-down numbers get built.

concerns.title: Passing game in freefall behind a sieve
concerns.body: Pass EPA ranks dead last, and the sack rate ranks 31st. The weekly line has been getting worse rather than stabilizing, ending at -14 passing EPA in Kansas City. With Alt out, there is no reason to expect protection to improve until he returns, and this is the real flaw, not noise.

concerns.title: Run-first plan without a run game
concerns.body: No team passes less than expected, yet the rushing attack is less efficient per play than the passing game. Yards before contact are only middling and the stuff rate ranks 22nd. The line is not opening anything, and the scheme is not compensating. This is a coaching choice that could change quickly, and it probably should.

concerns.title: Self-inflicted drive killers
concerns.body: Fifteen giveaways and 5.3 line penalties a game (32nd) wreck drives before the offense's talent can matter. The giveaways also inflate points allowed by gifting field position. Some of the turnover rate should regress, but the penalty problem has been steady and points to discipline and to a line playing hurt.

trend.note: The losses have been competitive but the passing game has deteriorated nearly every week. It bottomed out with 6 points and -14 passing EPA at Kansas City.

nextGame.headline: Off the bye, at a better-than-2-4 Rams team missing its front
nextGame.body:
This is a matchup of two of the league's unluckiest teams. The Rams are 2-4 with wins over expected ranked 31st, but they rank 9th in net EPA, 3rd in yards per game and 3rd in yards allowed. Their offense ranks 6th in success rate behind a line that allows pressure on 13.2% of dropbacks, the best rate in football. That neutralizes the Chargers' main defensive lever. The Chargers come in with 14 days of rest, the game is indoors, and the Book has not posted a line yet. The Rams' soft spots are special teams, ranked 32nd in EPA, and a pass rush that ranks 21st in pressure and 30th in QB hit rate.

Availability swings this game more than usual. The Rams have lost Kobie Turner (expected to IR) and Poona Ford (season) from the defensive front, and Myles Garrett is not having his practice window opened. They also lost kicker Blake Grupe to a torn ACL and Davante Adams until after their Week 11 bye, and Trent McDuffie sat the last game. On the Chargers' side, Joe Alt, Kayode Awosika, Tre' Harris, Derwin James and Donte Jackson are all listed out with return estimates of this very date, and McConkey is questionable in the concussion process. Whether Alt and James actually play is the biggest single factor.

waysToWin.title: Finally a clean pocket for Herbert
waysToWin.body: The Rams were already among the league's weakest at hitting the quarterback, and they have now lost three defensive linemen. This is the softest front the Chargers have seen. If Herbert gets time, the dropbacks that have been their worst plays become neutral or better, and the offense can stay ahead of the chains.

waysToWin.title: Field goals into a broken kicking game
waysToWin.body: The Chargers' red-zone and third-down defense forces kicks. The Rams have the league's worst special-teams EPA and just lost their kicker for the season. A low-scoring game decided by the kicking game suits the Chargers, who are winless in one-score games but 6th in red-zone touchdown defense.

waysToWin.title: Win the turnover battle for once
waysToWin.body: The Chargers' takeaway rate ranks 3rd and the Rams give it away more than they take it, ranking 20th in turnover margin. One or two short fields can flip a game the Chargers otherwise cannot win on yardage.

waysToLose.title: Rams march through a leaky deep secondary
waysToLose.body: The Rams' offense stays on schedule with a 6th-ranked success rate behind the best pass protection in the league. The Chargers' deep-pass defense ranks 25th and its explosive-pass rate allowed ranks 21st, and that gets worse if James and Jackson sit. Clean pockets plus coverage busts is how a 9th-ranked defense still gives up 25-plus.

waysToLose.title: Giveaways hand over short fields
waysToLose.body: The Chargers have multiple giveaways in all but one game, including four at Seattle. Against an offense this efficient, short fields turn into touchdowns, not the field goals this defense usually forces.

waysToLose.title: No vertical answer when they must pass
waysToLose.body: The Rams' deep-pass defense ranks 1st in EPA and its tight-end defense ranks 1st, which takes away Gadsden and the shot plays. If the Chargers fall behind, the run-first offense has nowhere to go. The one soft spot is the Rams' poor coverage of third receivers, but that depends on which Chargers wideouts are healthy.

nextGame.watch: Herbert's sacks and hits against a Rams front missing Turner, Ford and Garrett. If the Chargers cannot protect against this line, the offense's problem is structural, not opponent-driven.

restOfSeason.body:
The defense should keep playing at a top-ten level, and the -2.62 luck figure will not stay that extreme. Some of the one-score losses should start flipping, especially in the soft middle stretch against Houston, the Jets, Tampa Bay and a winless Miami. The takeaway pace will likely cool, which offsets part of that gain. Points allowed should drift down toward what the efficiency numbers say as the giveaways ease.

The ceiling is set by the offense. Getting Alt and Awosika back helps, but the protection and penalty problems predate this injury wave, and the run-heavy plan is not working on its own terms. If Harbaugh lets Herbert throw more once the line is whole, this can look like a mid-pack team down the stretch. If not, it is a 4- or 5-win season, with San Francisco, Kansas City and Denver closing it out.
swingFactors: Joe Alt's return and the line's health
Harbaugh opening up the passing game

confidence.note: Six games, heavy injuries, and return estimates that coincide with the next game.
